e.t: Abaian, also rendered Avean, is a proper name referring to a person. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 2 Chronicles 11:18. Because this is a personal name rather than a common noun or action word, its meaning is primarily identification: it distinguishes one individual from others in the passage. The name’s precise significance beyond identifying that person is not stated by the available lexical information.

This Greek LXX adverb describes acting in an ill-advised or inconsiderate way. It points to conduct carried out without sound judgment or proper thought for the consequences or for others. Because it is an adverb, it describes how an action is performed rather than naming a person, object, or event. This word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 1 Maccabees 5:67. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is clear: acting without wise consideration.

Ader, also identified as Ather, is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It functions as a personal name rather than a general word describing an object, action, or quality. The name occurs 39 times across 33 Old Testament verses, most often in 1 Kings. English rendering commonly preserves it as “Ader.” Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person being discussed.

Azōtia is a proper name, rendered as “Azōtia” or “Azotia.” It functions as a name rather than a word describing an action, quality, object, or relationship. In the Greek Old Testament data, it occurs once, at Nehemiah 13:23. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly identification: it points to the named entity in that passage, while the surrounding verse determines exactly what is being identified.

This Greek verb means “maltreat” or “torture,” describing the act of treating someone with cruel abuse or inflicting severe suffering. It is used five times in the Greek LXX corpus represented here, appearing in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. As a verb, it expresses an action done against another person rather than a quality or object. The surrounding passage determines the specific circumstances, but the central sense remains deliberate, harsh mistreatment.

This adjective describes something that is compulsory or indispensable—something required or necessary rather than optional. It can characterize a demand, condition, or matter that must be recognized because it cannot be left aside. In the Greek LXX corpus, the word occurs four times, in Wisdom, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular sentence depends on what the surrounding passage identifies as necessary or required.

This verb means “curse”: to speak or declare a curse against someone or something. In the Greek Old Testament, it describes the act of placing a person, city, or thing under a curse rather than merely expressing personal anger. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, including passages in Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the pronouncement of a curse.

e.h: To Shine or Come Into Sight
e.t: This Greek LXX verb means “shine up; sight”: it describes something becoming visible or appearing to the eye. As a verb, it expresses an action or change involving visibility rather than naming an object. It occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical material, including four occurrences in Job. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is appearing, becoming seen, or shining into view.

ἄνθρωπος means “person” or “human”: an individual human being, considered as a member of the human race. As a noun, it can refer to people generally or to a particular person, with the surrounding sentence determining which sense is intended. In the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical books represented here, it occurs 1,311 times, showing that it is a broad, ordinary word for human beings rather than a term limited to one special kind of person. Its precise reference depends on the passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “gush out” or “pour forth.” It describes something flowing outward in a strong or abundant way, rather than merely being present or remaining still. The word appears three times in the Greek text of Sirach, in Sirach 18:29, 39:6, and 50:27. Its exact force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its central idea remains the movement of something outward in a flowing stream or surge.

This word is the proper name “Antiochon,” also rendered “Antiokhon.” It refers to a person named Antiochon rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs 18 times across 18 verses in 1–4 Maccabees. The available material does not include verse text or surrounding context, so it cannot establish which Antiochon is intended in any particular occurrence. Its meaning is therefore the personal name itself.

This Greek LXX verb means “flee away”: it describes a person or thing moving away to escape or avoid something. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than naming a person, place, or object. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach 22:22. The precise force of the action in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and its context, but the word’s basic sense is clear: to flee away.

Areios is a proper name, identifying a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. Its listed gloss is “Areios; Arios,” giving two forms of the same name. Within the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 1 Maccabees, at 1 Maccabees 12:7 and 12:20. The name’s precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and narrative context.

gl: from the beginning; from of old
d: from the beginning; from of old

e.t: This adverb means “from the beginning” or “from of old.” It points backward to an earlier starting point or to something established in the distant past. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 3:21. Because the verse text is not included here, the surrounding passage determines whether the word emphasizes an original time, an ancient practice, or something known since long ago. Its basic time reference remains the same: it directs attention to what was true or present at an earlier beginning.

Asimoth is a proper name, rendered “Asimoth” in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 12:3. Because the available word-level information gives the name but not the surrounding verse text, it is best understood simply as the proper name Asimoth; its specific referent and significance belong to the context of that passage.

Astarōth is a proper name rendered “Astaroth.” It identifies a particular named entity rather than expressing a general quality, action, or object shared by many people. In the Greek Old Testament, the name occurs nine times, from Genesis through 1 Samuel, with several occurrences in Joshua. Its precise significance in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself functions as a name. The English form “Astaroth” preserves that identifying name rather than translating it into an ordinary descriptive term.

This word means “vapor”: a visible or perceptible form of moisture suspended in the air. It is a noun, naming something insubstantial rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs 11 times, appearing in both the Old Testament books and the deuterocanonical books represented here. The exact force of the word in any individual passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its ordinary lexical idea remains vapor.

This verb means to become unprofitable—that is, to come to be of no useful benefit. It describes a change into a condition where something or someone no longer serves a worthwhile purpose. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, across Psalms, Daniel, 2 Kings, and Jeremiah. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains becoming unprofitable rather than simply being called unprofitable.

This word is a proper name, represented by “Baddargis” or “Vaththaryis.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Joshua 15:61. The name itself does not provide enough information to determine whether the named entity is a person, place, or something else; that requires the surrounding verse and passage. Its role is therefore best understood as a name preserved in the Joshua record.

Balla, also rendered Valla, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a person in the Greek Old Testament translation. The name appears ten times, all in Genesis, so its use is limited to naming rather than expressing a broad concept. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the particular person or role associated with each occurrence cannot be explained from the name alone. The central meaning is simply the personal name Balla or Valla.

Bēthangabarim is a proper name referring to a place or location. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Nehemiah 3:16, and is also rendered Vithanggavarim. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding context, its precise location and significance cannot be stated here. The name itself functions as a place designation rather than a description, action, or quality.

This Greek LXX noun means “step” or “tribunal.” It can refer to a step or platform, or to a tribunal connected with judgment. Its precise sense depends on how it is used in the surrounding passage. The word occurs five times in the Greek Old Testament and deuterocanonical writings represented here, including Deuteronomy, Nehemiah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. These occurrences show that it is a concrete noun used for either a physical step or a place associated with judgment.

This word is a proper name, rendered “Bonni” or “Vonni.” It identifies a named individual rather than describing an action, quality, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 24:26. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not provided here, the name’s specific identity cannot be clarified further; its basic function is simply to designate the person named Bonni or Vonni.

This adjective describes something made of byblus. It identifies the material from which an object is made, rather than expressing an action, feeling, or quality apart from that material. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 18:2. Its specific reference there would require the surrounding verse text, but its ordinary meaning remains a material description: something manufactured from byblus.

This noun means “taste” or “tasting,” referring to the act or experience of perceiving something through the sense of taste. It can describe tasting food or another substance, whether focusing on the sensation itself or the act of sampling. In the Greek Old Testament material represented here, it occurs three times, all in the Wisdom of Solomon. Its precise force in any one sentence depends on what is being tasted and how the surrounding passage describes that experience.

Gibbir, also rendered Yivvir, is a proper name rather than a general word describing an idea, action, or quality. It identifies a specific person or place in the Greek Old Testament tradition. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, at Isaiah 10:31. The name alone does not establish the identity or significance of the person or place; those details depend on the surrounding verse and passage.

This adjective means “well-known,” describing someone or something recognized or familiar to others. It points to public awareness or established familiarity rather than describing a private thought or hidden quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages from Ruth, Samuel, Proverbs, Sirach, and 4 Maccabees. Its exact force—whether referring to a known person, relationship, or recognized matter—depends on the sentence in which it appears.

This Greek LXX verb means “rend” or “tear.” It describes the act of pulling or splitting something apart, whether the wording concerns a physical object or uses the action more broadly. The word occurs 80 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical writings, so it is a recurring verb rather than a rare expression. Its precise force in any passage depends on what is being torn and the surrounding sentence.

“Push asunder; tear away” is the basic meaning of this verb. It describes forcing something apart or pulling it away from its place. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 34:21. That single occurrence establishes its documented use in this corpus, while the surrounding verse context is needed to explain precisely what is being pushed apart or torn away there. The word therefore expresses forceful separation or removal rather than a gentle movement.

This word means a “present,” referring to something given to another person. It is a noun, so it names the gift itself rather than the act of giving. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Sirach 34:18. Its basic meaning is therefore simple and concrete: a present offered or received. The surrounding verse is needed to explain the particular point being made there, but the word itself identifies the gift. [Evidence: p03:word:lxx:L703903:identity; p03:word:lxx:L703903:occurrences; p01:word:lxx:L703903:reference:0]

This noun means an “inclosure” or “prison,” referring to a confined or enclosed place. It describes a physical setting that restricts movement rather than an action or personal quality. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Wisdom 17:15. Since the word appears only once and the verse text is not included here, its precise force in that passage must be understood from the surrounding context.

This verb means “oppress” or “squeeze out”: it describes forceful pressure placed on someone or something, often with the sense of driving it out or pressing it hard. As an action word, it focuses on what an oppressor does rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, showing this is a specific action expressed in several settings rather than a common general term. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding passage.

Ela is a proper name, referring to a particular person rather than expressing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, in 2 Samuel 23:29. The available lexical information identifies the name simply as “Ela,” without providing an additional meaning or description. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage context.

This adjective describes something continuous or perpetual—something that continues without interruption or comes to remain always. It functions as a description rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament collection, it occurs once, in Sirach 17:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic sense points to ongoing duration and persistence rather than something temporary or occasional.

This noun refers to the inward parts of the body—what a person might call the entrails or internal organs. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used especially for the inner portions of animals in sacrificial instructions, identifying the parts that were treated separately from the outer flesh. It also appears once in Sirach, but its basic meaning remains the same: the internal parts lying within the body. The word occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical text, most often in Exodus and Leviticus.

This word means “90,” the number ninety. It is an indeclinable number word, so it functions simply to state a numerical quantity rather than describe an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 20 times, most often in passages involving ages, counts, or quantities. Its basic meaning remains precise and consistent: ninety. The surrounding verse determines what is being counted or measured, but the word itself contributes only the numerical value.

This Greek LXX verb means “send forth”: to dispatch someone or something away from the sender toward a destination or purpose. It describes an act of sending, whether by a human authority or by God. The word appears 244 times in the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, so it commonly expresses movement initiated by a sender rather than movement occurring on its own. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on who sends and what or whom is sent.

This noun means “statement” or “narrative”—an expressed account, telling, or description. It refers to words arranged to communicate what is being said or related, rather than naming a person or action itself. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs twice: once in Judges and once in Sirach. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence and subject, but its basic sense remains an expressed account or statement.

This Greek LXX verb means “take hold/after”: it describes grasping, seizing, or coming after someone or something. Its basic idea is active movement toward another person or object, with the surrounding sentence showing whether the emphasis is on holding or following. The word appears 42 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it serves a range of ordinary actions rather than one narrow event. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

gl: that which is drawn over; curtain
d: that which is drawn over; curtain

e.t: This noun means “that which is drawn over; curtain.” It refers to a covering that can be pulled across or over something, functioning as a physical barrier or screen. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Exodus 26:36. The word’s basic sense is therefore a movable curtain or covering, while the surrounding passage determines exactly what it covers and how it functions there.

This LXX adverb means “before; in front of,” describing the position of something relative to another person or thing. It answers the question of where something is located or placed, rather than naming an object, person, or action. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in Job 26:6. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic idea remains a position directly before or in front of something.

This Greek LXX verb means “excite” or “irritate”: it describes stirring someone or something into an active, aroused, or disturbed response. Its basic sense can therefore cover provoking activity or provoking annoyance, depending on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, so it is used for more than one kind of situation. The exact force in any particular verse must be understood from that verse’s surrounding context.

Eskaiman, also rendered Eskeman, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies a named place or person in the Greek Old Testament text, but the available information does not specify which kind of name it is. This name occurs once, in Joshua 15:50. Its precise reference depends on the surrounding verse and passage, which are not included here.

This word is a personal name, rendered as “Esrikam” or “Ezrikam.” It identifies one individual rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or spiritual concept. In the Greek Old Testament corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:14. Because the available information gives the name but not the verse text or surrounding passage, its particular role in that genealogical or historical setting cannot be described further. The name’s meaning is therefore best stated simply: it is the proper name of a person.

This noun means “opportunity”—a suitable or favorable occasion for something to happen or be done. It refers to an opening in time or circumstances that can be recognized and used. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs five times, including in Psalms, Sirach, and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any verse depends on what action or situation the surrounding passage connects with that opportunity.

This verb means “prosper”: to do well, succeed, or experience favorable circumstances. It describes positive progress or flourishing rather than merely existing. In the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom text, it appears four times, including three occurrences in Leviticus and one in Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular sentence depends on what the surrounding passage says is prospering and how that success is described.

Zakchour, also rendered Zakkhur, is a personal name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies individuals in genealogical, priestly, musical, and community records. The name occurs eight times across eight verses, from Numbers through Nehemiah. Its specific significance belongs to the people who bore it; the name itself is not given a separate meaning in these passages.

This noun refers to “that which is laid down,” naming something set down rather than describing an action. It identifies a matter, arrangement, or standard that has been established. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs only twice, both times in 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense is therefore clear, though the precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse context. The word is a noun with a focused, relatively rare use in this corpus.

Ieglom is a proper name used for a person in the Greek Old Testament. It appears four times in total: three times in Genesis 36 and once in 1 Chronicles 1. The available wording identifies the name as “Ieglom,” but does not provide a broader definition or description of the person. Therefore, its meaning is chiefly its role as a personal name, while the surrounding verse context is needed to explain which individual is being mentioned in each passage.

Ieseri is a proper name, referring to a specific person or family designation rather than expressing a general quality, action, or idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Numbers 26:49. The available wording identifies the name but does not provide an additional definition or description. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and family-list context, which is handled separately from the word’s basic lexical identity.

This LXX noun refers to “jaundice” or “blight,” describing a damaging affliction. It can name a disease affecting the body or a destructive condition affecting plants and crops. The word occurs four times in the Greek Old Testament, in Leviticus, 2 Chronicles, Jeremiah, and Amos. Its precise reference—whether bodily illness or agricultural damage—depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is a harmful affliction that brings deterioration or loss.

Isobaam, also rendered Isovaam, is a proper name identifying a person. It is not a common word describing an action, quality, or object, so its meaning is chiefly the person designated by the name. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 14:4. The surrounding verse is needed to identify the person’s specific place in the passage; the name itself functions as a personal designation rather than as a general description.

Iōchabēd, also rendered Iokhavith, is a proper name belonging to a woman. It identifies a specific person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Samuel 14:3. The available lexical information establishes the name’s identity, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain what this person is doing or why she is mentioned there. Thus, its basic meaning is the personal name Iōchabēd, not a broader descriptive word.

This noun means a “vine-pole” or “vine-prop”—a support used to hold up or guide a vine. It names a practical object associated with cultivating grapevines, rather than an action or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, in 2 Maccabees 5:3. The surrounding verse text is not available here, so the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be described further.

This is a proper name, appearing in the Greek Old Testament as “Karchēdonioi” and “Karkhithoni.” It is not presented as an ordinary action, quality, or object word, but as a name used to identify a particular referent. The term occurs three times in the Greek LXX, all in Ezekiel: 27:12, 27:25, and 38:13. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain whom or what it identifies there.

This noun means “cataclysm”: a sudden, powerful, and destructive upheaval or disaster. It names an event marked by overwhelming devastation rather than an ordinary difficulty or isolated misfortune. In the Greek Old Testament and related LXX writings, it occurs 22 times, with many occurrences in Genesis and others in books such as Sirach, Psalms, Nahum, and 4 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a catastrophic event.

gl: get for oneself entirely; gain possession of
d: get for oneself entirely; gain possession of

e.t: This verb means to get something for oneself entirely or gain possession of it. It describes acquiring or securing something as one’s own, rather than merely seeing, using, or approaching it. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs twice: once in 2 Chronicles and once in 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in either passage depends on what is being acquired and the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains taking possession for oneself.

This Greek LXX verb means “count up” or “number”—to reckon people or things as part of a total. It occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Wisdom literature, with each occurrence appearing in a different passage: Isaiah 14:10, Daniel 5:17, and Wisdom 5:5. The word describes the act of assigning a count or reckoning something numerically, while the precise force in any one verse depends on its surrounding text.

This verb means “despise”: to regard someone or something with contempt, treating it as unworthy of respect or attention. It expresses a serious attitude of disregard rather than simple dislike. As a verb, it describes the action of looking down on or rejecting the value of another person, instruction, or thing. This LXX word occurs 20 times, showing that it is used across several kinds of passages while retaining this central sense.

This Greek LXX noun means “thunderbolt,” referring to a powerful flash or bolt associated with a storm. It names a visible force from the heavens rather than describing a person, action, or inward quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here: once in Job and once each in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse, but its basic meaning remains a thunderbolt.

Kechar, also rendered Kekhar, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, at 2 Samuel 18:23. The available wording preserves it as a name, but does not provide an additional meaning or explanation of whom or what it identifies. Its precise significance therefore depends on the surrounding passage and the person or place named there.

This word means a barber or hair-cutter—a person whose work is cutting hair. It is a noun naming the person who performs that task, rather than the haircut or the tool used. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Ezekiel 5:1. Its basic meaning remains straightforward, while the precise significance of its use there depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This LXX adverb means “secretly,” describing an action done out of public view or without others knowing. It tells how something happens rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Scriptures represented in this corpus, including passages from Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Judges, Ruth, Isaiah, and Wisdom. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains concealed or unobserved action.

This noun means “hindrance” or “impediment”: something that gets in the way or prevents a person from moving forward. It describes an obstacle rather than an action, person, or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament, the Septuagint, it occurs once, at Job 13:27. The word’s basic sense remains focused on whatever obstructs, restrains, or blocks progress; its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording and passage.

This noun means “performance of a,” referring to the carrying out of an assigned act or duty. It describes something being performed rather than a person or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers, showing a focused use connected with an appointed activity. The surrounding verse supplies the specific thing being performed; the word itself emphasizes the act of carrying it out.

gl: in the north; on the left hand
d: in the north; on the left hand

e.t: This noun refers to a position or direction: “in the north” or “on the left hand.” It identifies location rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:27. The wording can describe either northern location or the left-hand side, so the surrounding passage determines which sense is intended there. Its basic meaning remains a directional description of where something is situated.

Meth is a proper name, identifying someone or something called Meth rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:20. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise role in that passage cannot be stated safely. The name itself is clear, but understanding whom or what it identifies requires reading the surrounding passage in context.

Mekedō, also rendered Meketho, is a proper name referring to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It appears once in the Greek LXX, at 1 Kings 4:12. Because the name is not a common noun or descriptive term, it does not by itself express an action, quality, or doctrine. Its precise identification and significance in that passage depend on the surrounding verse and passage context.

Melchisedek is a proper name identifying a particular person in the Greek Old Testament. The name appears twice in this corpus, once in Genesis 14:18 and once in Psalms 109:4. Because it is a personal name rather than a common noun or action word, its basic meaning is the person it names. The spelling “Melkhisethek” is another supplied rendering of the same name. The name itself does not describe a general quality or activity; its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This Greek LXX preposition means “with” or “amid,” expressing association or being in the midst of something. It commonly links a person or thing with others, or places someone or something among surrounding people or circumstances. The word occurs 2,137 times in the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical books, showing that it is a common relational word rather than a term limited to one setting. Its exact force in a verse depends on what people, things, or circumstances it connects.

This adjective means “stained,” describing something marked or soiled. Its basic sense points to a condition of being defiled or carrying a blemish, whether the surrounding passage applies it to a person, object, or situation. In the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, it occurs 11 times across 11 verses. The precise force—whether literal or figurative—depends on the sentence and surrounding passage where it appears.

Nabai, also rendered Nave, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it identifies a person named in Judges 8:11. This name occurs once in the LXX corpus, so Scripture provides no broader range of uses for it. Its significance in that verse must be understood from the surrounding passage, while the name itself functions simply as a personal designation.

Nōdab, also given as Nothav, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. This name occurs once in the Greek Septuagint, at 2 Samuel 6:6. Because the available information identifies the name but does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its particular role in that verse cannot be described here. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the personal name itself.

This verb means to be in pain or to experience pain. It describes suffering that is felt personally, whether physical or inward. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears ten times, so its basic sense is consistent across several books rather than limited to one passage. The word can describe someone who suffers or express the condition of being pained. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding wording, but the central idea remains pain and distress.

Profit refers to gain or benefit received from something. As a noun, this word names an advantage or useful return rather than an action. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Zechariah 8:10. That single occurrence establishes its lexical sense, while the surrounding verse would be needed to explain exactly what kind of profit is meant there. The word therefore points generally to beneficial gain, with its precise force determined by the sentence and passage in which it appears.

This verb means “impassioned; anger”: it describes becoming strongly moved by anger or acting from an intense emotional response. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it is used broadly rather than for one isolated kind of situation. It occurs 71 times in this LXX corpus, including passages from Genesis through 4 Maccabees. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Ulam is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name is rendered “Ulam” and appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in 1 Chronicles 7:16–17. Because it is a personal name, its meaning is its identification of the individual called Ulam; the surrounding verse text would be needed to explain that person’s specific place in the passage.

This word means “sky” or “heaven,” referring to the expanse above the earth. As a noun, it can describe the visible sky or the heavenly realm, depending on the surrounding passage. It is broadly used throughout the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, occurring 578 times. Its use begins in Genesis 1:1 and continues through the Epistle of Jeremiah. The word therefore covers both the ordinary heavens seen above and the higher heavenly sphere spoken of in Scripture.

This Greek LXX verb means “encourage”: to give someone strength, courage, or renewed resolve. It describes an action directed toward another person, rather than merely expressing a feeling within oneself. In this corpus, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 13:8. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a supportive act of strengthening or heartening someone. The context determines whether that encouragement comes through words, presence, or an appeal.
